title: Building a SaaS product in India: tenancy, GST, billing
description: Building a SaaS product in India: silo or pool tenancy, PostgreSQL row security, GST LUT for exports, and RBI's ₹15,000 e-mandate rule for billing.

faq.q: What is multi-tenancy in a SaaS product?
faq.a: It means one product serves many customer organisations, called tenants, while keeping each one's data separate. AWS describes three ways to do it: silo (dedicated resources per tenant), pool (shared resources) and bridge (a mix).

faq.q: Should a small SaaS start with one database per customer?
faq.a: Usually not. A pooled database with a tenant id on every row and database row security is cheaper to run and faster to update. Give a customer its own database when a contract requires it and the price covers the extra work.

faq.q: Do I charge GST when I sell SaaS to a customer outside India?
faq.a: If the sale meets all five conditions of section 2(6) of the IGST Act, it is an export of services and zero rated. You can export without paying IGST by filing an LUT in Form GST RFD-11. Confirm the place of supply and payment conditions with your CA.

faq.q: How long is a GST LUT valid?
faq.a: The GST portal user guide says the LUT status changes to expired at the end of the financial year. File a new one each year before your first export invoice.

faq.q: Can I auto-charge an Indian customer's card every month?
faq.a: Yes, through an e-mandate set up by your payment gateway. Under RBI's E-mandate Framework, 2026, charges up to ₹15,000 need no additional authentication, and the customer gets a notice at least 24 hours before each debit.

faq.q: What happens if my annual plan costs more than ₹15,000?
faq.a: The customer has to authenticate the renewal charge. Send a reminder before the renewal date and handle a failed charge in the product, so the account is not locked without warning.

faq.q: Is PostgreSQL row-level security enough on its own?
faq.a: No. It is a safety net under your application's own tenant checks. It also does nothing if your app connects as a superuser, a BYPASSRLS role or the table owner, unless you force row security on the table.

contentHtml:
What building a SaaS product in India involves

In short: Building a SaaS product in India means three decisions most founders make too late. How tenants share the database (silo, pool or bridge), how GST works when you sell abroad (an LUT in Form GST RFD-11 lets you export without paying IGST), and how Indian recurring billing works under RBI's e-mandate rules (no extra authentication up to ₹15,000 a charge, and a notice 24 hours before every debit).

This guide was checked in November 2026, against the official pages listed at the end. I am not a chartered accountant or a lawyer. The tax sections tell you what the law and the GST portal say, so you can have a sharper conversation with your CA. They are not tax advice.

The three decisions at a glance

Before any detail, here is the whole map. Each row is a decision that is cheap to make on day one and expensive to change after a year of customer data.

Three early decisions for an Indian SaaS product, and where the rule comes from

DecisionYour optionsWhat the official source saysWhen it bites
How tenants share infrastructureSilo, pool or bridgeAWS's SaaS Lens: silo gives tenants dedicated resources, pool shares them, bridge mixes bothYour first large customer asks for its own database
Keeping tenants apart in a shared databaseApplication filters, or database row-level securityPostgreSQL: with row security on and no policy, a default-deny policy is usedA query forgets its tenant filter
GST on sales to foreign customersPay IGST and claim a refund, or export under an LUTGST portal: file the LUT in Form GST RFD-11 before making the supply; it expires at the end of the financial yearYour first invoice to a customer outside India
Recurring billing for Indian customersCards, UPI AutoPay or e-mandate through a gatewayRBI's E-mandate Framework, 2026: no AFA up to ₹15,000 per charge, notice 24 hours before each debitYour first annual plan priced above ₹15,000

Source: AWS SaaS Lens and PostgreSQL documentation and GST portal user guide and RBI E-mandate Framework, 2026, read 16 November 2026.

I put the tax and billing rows next to the architecture rows on purpose. Founders often treat them as separate worlds. They are not. Your invoice needs to know the customer's country, your billing system needs to know the plan amount, and both need to know the tenant. One clean tenant model feeds all three.

Silo, pool or bridge: how tenants share your product

AWS's SaaS Lens gives the clearest vocabulary I have found. The silo model "refers to an architecture where tenants are provided dedicated resources," for example a separate database per tenant. The pool model "refers to a scenario where tenants share resources," which AWS calls "the more classic notion of multi-tenancy." The bridge model admits that most real products are "not always exclusively silo or pool" and mix the two.

One line in that page matters for Indian agencies and software shops. AWS says a silo still runs on "a shared identity, onboarding, and operational experience." If every client has its own copy of the code, its own login system and its own deployment, you are not running SaaS. You are running managed hosting for many separate products. That is a fine business, but it does not get cheaper as you add customers.

Here is how I would weigh them for a small Indian SaaS business.

  • Pool is the default for most products sold to small businesses. One database, one deployment, a tenant id on every row. It is the cheapest to run and the fastest to ship updates to everyone. The risk is that one bug can show one tenant's data to another.
  • Silo suits a handful of large customers who pay for it: a hospital chain that wants its own database, or an enterprise whose security team asks for it in writing. You pay in operations: every migration runs many times.
  • Bridge is where most products end up. Pool for the small plans, silo for the database of one or two premium customers, shared login and billing for everyone.

AWS's older tenant isolation whitepaper is now marked "for historical reference only," but its point still holds: decide isolation per resource. Your file storage can be pooled with a tenant prefix while one customer's database is siloed.

Keeping tenants apart in a shared database

In a pooled database, the whole product depends on one rule: every query must carry the tenant. The usual way is a tenant_id column on every table and a WHERE tenant_id = ? in every query. That works until someone writes a report query at 11 pm and forgets the filter.

PostgreSQL has a second line of defence built in. Its row security documentation says that once row-level security is enabled on a table, "all normal access to the table for selecting rows or modifying rows must be allowed by a row security policy." And: "If no policy exists for the table, a default-deny policy is used, meaning that no rows are visible or can be modified." A forgotten filter returns nothing instead of returning everyone's data.

The same page has the catch that I see missed most often. "Superusers and roles with the BYPASSRLS attribute always bypass the row security system when accessing a table. Table owners normally bypass row security as well." If your application connects to the database as the user that owns the tables, which is the default in many quick setups, your policies do nothing. The fix is to connect as a separate role, or to use ALTER TABLE ... FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY, which the documentation describes for exactly this case.

A five-minute test worth running

Log in to your app as a user of tenant A. Copy the id of any record from tenant B out of the database. Paste it into a URL or API call in tenant A's session. If you see tenant B's record, your isolation depends on luck. Run this test before every major release.

GST when you sell SaaS to customers outside India

Many Indian SaaS founders sell to customers in the US, UK, UAE or elsewhere from early on. That sale can be an export of services under GST, which is zero rated. But it only counts as an export if every condition in the law is met.

Section 2(6) of the IGST Act, 2017 says "export of services" means the supply of any service when all of these hold:

  • the supplier of service is located in India;
  • the recipient of service is located outside India;
  • the place of supply of service is outside India;
  • the payment for such service has been received by the supplier of service in convertible foreign exchange or in Indian rupees wherever permitted by the Reserve Bank of India; and
  • the supplier of service and the recipient of service are not merely establishments of a distinct person.

For a SaaS product, the third and fourth conditions are the ones that need care. The place of supply has its own rules in the IGST Act, and your CA should confirm it for your type of service. The payment condition means your billing setup decides part of your tax position: money has to arrive in a way that meets it.

When the sale is an export, you have two routes. You can pay IGST and claim a refund, or you can furnish a Letter of Undertaking and export without paying IGST. The GST portal user guide says registered taxpayers with zero-rated supplies "have to furnish LUT in Form GST RFD-11 on the GST Portal before affecting such supply." The menu path it gives is Services, then User Services, then Furnish Letter of Undertaking (LUT).

Three details from that guide that founders miss:

  • The LUT's status changes to expired at the end of the financial year. You file a fresh one each year, ideally in early April before your first invoice.
  • It needs two independent witnesses with name, address and occupation, and the authorised signatory signs with DSC or EVC.
  • You are eligible only if you have not been prosecuted for tax evasion of ₹2.5 crore or more.

The CBIC master circular on LUT and bond (Circular No. 8/8/2017-GST) is the older official reference behind these steps, if your CA wants the paper trail.

One more rule touches growing SaaS businesses. From 1 August 2023, e-invoicing applies to taxpayers with aggregate turnover above ₹5 crore in any preceding financial year from 2017-18, according to EY’s alert on Notification No. 10/2023. If you are close to that number, your billing system needs to generate invoices that can be reported through the e-invoice system. That is far easier to design in than to bolt on.

Recurring billing for Indian customers under RBI's e-mandate rules

Billing Indian customers every month is not like billing a US card on file. The Digital Payments: E-mandate Framework, 2026, issued by RBI on 21 April 2026 and effective immediately, covers recurring transactions "using cards / PPI / UPI." The rules that change how you design plans:

  • The ₹15,000 line. Clause 8(a): "All recurring transactions may be authorised without AFA up to ₹15,000/- per transaction." Above that, the customer has to authenticate the charge again. Insurance premiums, mutual fund subscriptions and credit card bills get a higher limit of ₹1,00,000, but a SaaS subscription is not in that list.
  • The 24-hour notice. Clause 6(a): the issuer sends a pre-transaction notification "at least 24 hours prior to the actual charge / debit."
  • Opt-out at any time. Clause 6(c): customers get a facility to opt out of any particular transaction or the whole mandate.

You will not build this yourself. A gateway handles the mandate. Razorpay’s Subscriptions documentation, for example, lists cards, UPI AutoPay and e-mandates "via Aadhaar, netbanking or debit card-based mandates." Stripe’s India recurring payments guide puts the practical result plainly: recurring transactions over 15,000 INR must go through AFA each time, and customers receive a pre-debit notice at least 24 hours before the payment.

What this means for your product design:

  • An annual plan priced at ₹24,000 will ask the customer to authenticate at renewal. Expect some renewals to fail quietly. Build a reminder email and a retry flow before the renewal date, not after.
  • A monthly plan at ₹2,000 can renew without AFA, but your app still needs to handle a customer opting out of one charge.
  • Your tenant record needs a billing state (trial, active, past due, cancelled) that the product checks. Without it, a failed charge leaves a tenant using the product free for months.

How to set it up, step by step

This is the order I would follow for a new product, or for an existing single-customer product being turned into SaaS.

Step 1. Write down your tenant. A tenant is usually a company or a clinic, not a person. Decide whether one user can belong to two tenants (an accountant serving five firms can). This one sentence shapes your login design.

Step 2. Add the tenant id everywhere. Every table that holds customer data gets a tenant_id column, not null, with an index. Files go under a tenant prefix in storage. Background jobs carry the tenant id in their payload.

Step 3. Turn on database row security. On PostgreSQL, enable row-level security on each tenant table, add a policy keyed to the current tenant, and connect the app as a role that is not the table owner. Then run the five-minute test above.

Step 4. Decide who gets a silo. Default everyone to pool. Write down the condition for a silo (a contract that requires it, a data volume that hurts others) and a price for it. Large customers will ask.

Step 5. Store the customer's country and GSTIN on the tenant. Your invoice logic needs both: an Indian business customer with a GSTIN, an Indian customer without one, and a foreign customer are three different invoices. Ask your CA to approve the three templates.

Step 6. File the LUT before your first export invoice. Do it on the GST portal in Form GST RFD-11, and put a reminder in your calendar for every April.

Step 7. Choose a gateway and test a renewal above ₹15,000. Use the gateway's test mode to see what the customer experiences when a charge needs AFA. Design the email that goes out before it.

Step 8. Log every tenant action with the tenant id. When a customer says their data changed, you need to find who did it, in which tenant, at what time. Our post on app monitoring and logs in India covers the logging side.

Worked examples for three Indian SaaS businesses

These examples are illustrative. The businesses and numbers are invented to show the decisions, not taken from real clients.

A clinic management app sold to clinics in Telangana

Say a founder in Hyderabad built appointment and billing software for one clinic and now wants to sell it to forty. Every clinic is a tenant. Patients are not tenants, they are records inside a clinic. Pool fits: forty small clinics on one database, row security on every table, the clinic id in every file path for prescriptions and reports.

Health data makes isolation matter more, not less. A doctor in one clinic seeing another clinic's patient list is the failure that ends the business. I would run the tenant A and tenant B test before every release. Billing is monthly and small, so it renews under ₹15,000 without AFA, but the app still needs to lock a clinic out gently when payment fails, without hiding its existing patient records. Our page on healthcare app development has more on this sector.

An HR and payroll tool sold to companies in the UAE and UK

Say a Pune team sells an HR tool mostly to customers outside India. The GST side comes first. Each foreign customer's invoice needs to meet the section 2(6) export conditions, and the team files its LUT every April so it can invoice without IGST. Payment has to arrive in a way that meets the foreign exchange condition, which is a question for the CA and the bank before the first invoice, not after.

One UK customer with 2,000 employees asks for its own database. That is the bridge model: shared login, onboarding and billing, a siloed database for that customer at a price that covers the extra migrations and backups.

A learning platform sold to coaching institutes

Say a coaching institute owner in Vijayawada built a test series app and now sells it to other institutes. Each institute is a tenant. Students may belong to two institutes, so the login model needs a user who can switch between tenants. Videos and question banks are large files, stored under a tenant prefix.

Some institutes want an annual plan at ₹36,000. Under the RBI rules that renewal needs the customer to authenticate again. The founder offers a monthly plan at ₹3,000 that renews without AFA, plus the annual plan with a renewal reminder seven days ahead. Our education app page covers this sector.

Ways this goes wrong

  • Treating each client as a separate copy. Forty copies of the code means forty deployments for every fix. Founders discover this when a security patch takes a week.
  • Row security that the app user bypasses. Policies are written, tests pass, and the app connects as the table owner. PostgreSQL's own documentation says owners normally bypass row security.
  • Forgetting the background jobs. The web app filters by tenant. The nightly report job does not, and emails one customer's numbers to another.
  • No LUT in April. The LUT expires at the end of the financial year. The first export invoice in April goes out without one.
  • Assuming any foreign payment counts as an export. The payment condition in section 2(6) has to be met. Check how your gateway or bank settles the money.
  • Annual plans that silently fail to renew. Above ₹15,000 the customer must authenticate. Without a reminder, the charge fails and nobody notices until the tenant complains that the product stopped working.
  • No billing state on the tenant. Failed payments never reach the product, so unpaid tenants keep full access.

A checklist before your tenth customer

  • Every customer table has a not-null tenant id with an index.
  • Row-level security is on, and the app does not connect as the table owner or a BYPASSRLS role.
  • The tenant A and tenant B test passes on web, mobile and API.
  • Background jobs, exports and reports carry and check the tenant id.
  • Files are stored under a tenant prefix and served only after a tenant check.
  • You have a written rule and price for when a customer gets a silo.
  • Each tenant record stores country, GSTIN if any, plan and billing state.
  • Your CA has approved invoice templates for domestic and export customers.
  • This year's LUT is filed on the GST portal, and next April is in the calendar.
  • A renewal above ₹15,000 has been tested end to end in gateway test mode.
  • Logs record the tenant id and user id for every change.
  • Code, cloud accounts and the gateway account are in the company's name, not a developer's.

If you want this worked out for your product before anything is built, our ₹3,500 requirement analysis is a call with the people who would build it, the requirements worked through, and a written fixed quotation and timeline (book it here). Code, cloud and credentials stay in your name. For broader context on product builds, see our SaaS development service page.

Frequently asked questions

What is multi-tenancy in a SaaS product?

It means one product serves many customer organisations, called tenants, while keeping each one's data separate. AWS describes three ways to do it: silo (dedicated resources per tenant), pool (shared resources) and bridge (a mix).

Should a small SaaS start with one database per customer?

Usually not. A pooled database with a tenant id on every row and database row security is cheaper to run and faster to update. Give a customer its own database when a contract requires it and the price covers the extra work.

Do I charge GST when I sell SaaS to a customer outside India?

If the sale meets all five conditions of section 2(6) of the IGST Act, it is an export of services and zero rated. You can export without paying IGST by filing an LUT in Form GST RFD-11. Confirm the place of supply and payment conditions with your CA.

How long is a GST LUT valid?

The GST portal user guide says the LUT status changes to expired at the end of the financial year. File a new one each year before your first export invoice.

Can I auto-charge an Indian customer's card every month?

Yes, through an e-mandate set up by your payment gateway. Under RBI's E-mandate Framework, 2026, charges up to ₹15,000 need no additional authentication, and the customer gets a notice at least 24 hours before each debit.

What happens if my annual plan costs more than ₹15,000?

The customer has to authenticate the renewal charge. Send a reminder before the renewal date and handle a failed charge in the product, so the account is not locked without warning.

Is PostgreSQL row-level security enough on its own?

No. It is a safety net under your application's own tenant checks. It also does nothing if your app connects as a superuser, a BYPASSRLS role or the table owner, unless you force row security on the table.
